results.result: The authors established a human co-culture system using tumor cells and primary immune cells to investigate tumor evasion mechanisms. CMV-specific CTLs were expanded from PBMCs, achieving a 39.4-fold expansion (0.64±0.02% to 25.1±2.88%) after 8 days. These CTLs killed antigen-loaded tumor cells in a dose-dependent manner, and B2M KO cells were resistant, confirming MHCI-dependent killing. A CRISPRa system was validated in HCT 116 cells, successfully inducing expression of CD274, CD80, and NT5E.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C70 describe the experimental system and validation experiments. The CTL expansion data (C57) is quantitative with error bars. The antigen-dependent killing (C62-C64) is demonstrated with appropriate controls (B2M KO). The CRISPRa validation (C65-C70) shows successful gene induction. These foundational experiments are well-controlled and support the establishment of the screening system.

results.result: Complementary CRISPRa and CRISPR KO screens were performed using sgRNA libraries targeting ~10,000 genes in HCT 116 cells. The screens identified 187 hits (CRISPRa) and 704 hits (CRISPR KO), with 60 overlapping genes. Control screens showed expected depletion of essential genes (RNA processing, cell cycle, spliceosome) in KO and genes affecting cell homeostasis (calcium signaling, ABC transporters) in CRISPRa. Tumor killing of 74% (KO) and 91% (CRISPRa) was achieved after 3 days co-culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C84 describe the screen design, execution, and quality control. The quantitative hit numbers are clearly stated. The control screens (C76-C81) show expected results for essential genes, validating screen quality. The differential killing percentages (C83-C84) demonstrate appropriate selection pressure. The genome-wide coverage (C82) and library sizes (C71-C72) are well-documented.

results.result: The complementary screens confirmed previously identified pathways (IFN-γ, TNF-α, autophagy) and identified novel genes. Key validated genes include PTPN2, SOCS1, STAT1, JAK2 (IFN-γ pathway); TNFRSF1A, MAP3K7, CFLAR (TNF-α pathway); and ATG3, ATG10, ATG12, ATG13 (autophagy). Top overlapping hits (PTPN2, CFLAR, CHD7, ILKAP) showed bidirectional effects: increased sensitivity when depleted and resistance when activated. ICAM1 and JAK2 showed opposite patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C94 describe pathway validation and hit identification. The confirmation of known pathways (C50-C52, C93-C94) validates the screen approach. The bidirectional effects of overlapping hits (C86-C91) are logically consistent with the complementary screen design. The identification of novel genes (C13) is supported by the screen data, though specific validation experiments are needed for individual hits.

results.result: Genes regulating antigen processing and presentation were not enriched in the screens, attributed to direct peptide loading on tumor cells. TAK1 inhibitor (Takinib) significantly enhanced tumor killing in a dose-dependent manner, validating the role of TNF-α signaling in tumor resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide mechanistic insight and validation. The absence of antigen presentation genes (C95) is explained by the experimental design (direct peptide loading), which is logical. The TAK1 inhibitor experiment (C96-C97) provides orthogonal validation of TNF-α pathway involvement with dose-response data, strengthening the screen findings.

results.result: ICAM-1 deletion induced resistance to CTL killing in all three cell lines tested (HCT 116, Panc-1, UACC-257), independent of antigen presentation (HLA-A2 levels unchanged). LFA-1 was present on CTLs. PD-L1 overexpression had minimal effect on killing, and PD-1/PD-L1 interaction showed little role in activated CTL-tumor cell interaction. ICAM-1 depletion had greater effect than PD-L1 overexpression in inducing resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C109 establish ICAM-1's role in CTL-mediated killing. The validation across multiple cell lines (C103) strengthens the finding. The control experiments showing unchanged HLA-A2 (C104) rule out antigen presentation effects. The comparison with PD-L1 (C106, C109) is well-controlled with appropriate antibody blocking experiments. The presence of LFA-1 on CTLs (C102) supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Multiple ICAM-1 isoforms exist, including soluble variants. Mutations Y474A+Y485A and P404E, previously shown to inhibit ICAM-1 shedding in other cell types, did not alter mICAM-1 or sICAM-1 levels in HCT 116 cells. Transfection experiments showed differential expression: sICAM1 transfection increased supernatant sICAM-1 5.21±0.42 fold in KO cells; full-length ICAM1 increased sICAM-1 2.21±0.11 fold; ICAM1 KO cells secreted 4-fold less sICAM-1 than WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C122 characterize ICAM-1 isoforms and shedding. The negative results with Y474A+Y485A and P404E mutations (C117-C118) are appropriately reported and indicate cell-type-specific mechanisms. The quantitative measurements of sICAM-1 levels (C119-C122) are precise with error bars. The equal transfection efficiency (C115) validates the comparison between constructs.

results.result: Full-length ICAM1 rescued CTL-mediated killing in ICAM1 KO cells. P404E mutant rescued killing similarly to full-length, but Y474A+Y485A did not. sICAM-1 overexpression in WT cells protected from killing, but external addition of sICAM-1 (conditioned medium or recombinant) had no effect. ICAM1-ΔC (cytoplasmic tail deleted) rescued killing like full-length, but GPI-anchored ICAM-1 was less efficient. mICAM-1 promotes killing while sICAM-1 increases resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C136 demonstrate opposing roles of ICAM-1 isoforms. The rescue experiments (C123-C125) are well-controlled with multiple constructs. The requirement for cell-intrinsic sICAM-1 production (C128-C131) is demonstrated through negative results with external addition. The domain mapping experiments (C132-C133) provide mechanistic insight. The conclusion about opposing roles (C134-C136) is supported by the collective data.

results.result: TNF-α and IFN-γ enhanced mICAM-1 expression and induced sICAM-1 release in all tested cell lines, with synergistic effects when combined. TCGA/GTEx analysis showed ICAM1 expression in all normal tissues at varying levels, with significant upregulation in 12 cancer types. MMP9 was elevated in all tumor types; ADAM10 and ADAM17 were increased in some tumors; ELANE and CTSG were lower in tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C147 connect experimental findings to clinical data. The cytokine stimulation experiments (C138-C140) demonstrate regulation across multiple cell lines. The TCGA analysis (C143-C147) provides large-scale validation with appropriate statistical comparisons between tumor and normal tissue. The generalizability claim (C141) is supported by testing multiple cell lines.

results.result: High co-expression of ICAM1 with MMP9 was associated with shorter survival in glioblastoma multiforme. High co-expression of ICAM1 with ADAM10 or ADAM17 was associated with poor outcome in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Combined expression of ICAM1 and proteases had worse impact on survival than individual genes alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C152 establish clinical relevance through survival analysis. The survival associations (C148-C149) are cancer-type-specific with statistical significance. The synergistic effect of combined expression (C150) strengthens the mechanistic model. However, these are correlative analyses that cannot establish causation, and the quartile-based grouping may introduce bias.

results.result: CTL-mediated tumor killing is modulated by mICAM-1 levels and sICAM-1 release. mICAM-1 contributes to productive immunological synapse formation leading to killing, while ICAM-1 absence or sICAM-1 release inhibits killing.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C155 synthesize the ICAM-1 findings into a mechanistic model. This conclusion is well-supported by the collective experimental data showing opposing effects of membrane-bound and soluble forms. The model integrates multiple lines of evidence including knockout, overexpression, and isoform-specific experiments.

results.result: ILKAP, encoding integrin-linked kinase-associated serine/threonine phosphatase 2C, was identified as a novel regulator of tumor resistance. ILKAP depletion increased tumor sensitivity to CTL killing in HCT 116 and Panc-1 cells, correlating with remaining expression. ILKAP-mediated resistance was independent of IFN-γ/TNF-α sensitivity, antigen presentation, and PD-L1 levels. ILKAP KO cells showed enhanced basal ICAM-1 levels. ILKAP overexpression had minor impact on ICAM-1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C171 establish ILKAP as a novel regulator. The validation across two cell lines (C156-C158) with dose-response correlation strengthens the finding. The mechanistic characterization (C159-C162) appropriately rules out known pathways. The connection to ICAM-1 (C161, C165) is intriguing but preliminary. The authors appropriately note that further investigation is needed (C167). The novelty claim (C15) appears accurate based on literature.

results.result: ILKAP was previously identified as an ILK1 regulator in Wnt signaling and associated with cisplatin resistance in ovarian cancer, but not with CTL-mediated killing. ILK regulates ICAM-1 via NF-κB signaling. The authors propose ILKAP regulates ICAM-1 basal levels through ILK signaling, based on trends with catalytic inactive mutant. The minor overexpression effect may reflect high basal ILKAP activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C178 provide mechanistic speculation. The prior literature (C172-C175) is appropriately cited. However, the proposed mechanism (C176) is based on trends rather than statistically significant effects (C163 reports "non-significant decrease"). The explanation for asymmetric effects (C177) is speculative. The independence from known pathways (C178) is better supported. More direct mechanistic experiments are needed.

results.result: ICAM-1 plays multiple immune roles including T cell activation and leukocyte recruitment. Surface ICAM-1 binds LFA-1 and contributes to immunological synapse formation during CTL killing and T cell priming. From the tumor side, ICAM-1 is important for physical interaction with minimal signaling function. ICAM1-ΔC (lacking cytoplasmic domain) rescued killing like full-length, but GPI-anchored ICAM-1 did not, suggesting membrane self-association and distribution are crucial. Dimerization and clustering enhance LFA-1 binding affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C187 integrate prior knowledge with new findings. The domain mapping experiments (C184-C185) provide mechanistic insight into ICAM-1 function. The differential rescue by ΔC versus GPI-anchored forms (C184-C185) supports the importance of membrane organization over cytoplasmic signaling. The interpretation is consistent with cited literature on ICAM-1 clustering (C186-C187).

results.result: sICAM-1 inhibits tumor killing. The protective effect requires cell-intrinsic sICAM-1 production, not external addition, suggesting high local concentration at the immunological synapse may be needed. The pro-tumorigenic function of sICAM-1 may explain lack of selective pressure for ICAM-1 loss. Tumor killing may be regulated by the mICAM-1/sICAM-1 ratio. Upregulation of ICAM1 in cancers should result in sICAM-1 release, favoring tumor growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C193 propose a model for sICAM-1 function. The requirement for cell-intrinsic production (C189) is well-demonstrated through negative controls. The local concentration hypothesis (C190) is reasonable speculation. The evolutionary argument (C191) is logical but speculative. The ratio model (C192) integrates the findings well. The inference about cancer (C193) follows from the experimental data and TCGA analysis.

results.result: Clinical data show sICAM-1 is upregulated in CRC and lung cancer patients with poor prognosis. IFN-1-induced ICAM-1 can surmount PD-L1/PD-1 axis. The authors propose therapeutic strategies: (1) immune checkpoint blockade to enhance mICAM-1 over sICAM-1; (2) selective MMP-9, ADAM10, or ADAM17 inhibitors to prevent ICAM-1 cleavage; (3) pH-dependent "sweeping" antibodies to deplete sICAM-1. Previous metalloprotease inhibitor trials failed due to side effects or lack of benefit, but newer selective inhibitors might succeed.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C205 discuss clinical implications and therapeutic proposals. The clinical associations (C194-C195) are supported by cited literature. The therapeutic proposals (C197-C198, C202-C203) are speculative and not tested in this study. The sweeping antibody concept (C203-C205) is interesting but entirely speculative. The discussion of prior metalloprotease inhibitor failures (C199-C201) provides important context. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but lack experimental support.

results.result: The impact of mICAM-1 and sICAM-1 on myeloid cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) and their effect on CTL killing is unclear. sICAM-1 stimulates myeloid cell recruitment. Membrane ICAM-1 on dendritic cells facilitates T cell priming and CTL survival/memory, while soluble form may have opposing effects. ICAM-1 regulates macrophage polarization, affecting CTL killing. Further studies are needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C212 discuss gaps in understanding and cite relevant literature. These are appropriate acknowledgments of study limitations and areas for future research. The cited effects on dendritic cells (C208) and macrophages (C210-C211) are from prior literature. The speculation about opposing effects of soluble form (C209) is reasonable but untested. This represents honest discussion of what remains unknown.

results.result: CTLs are key players in anti-tumor immunity, and many immunotherapies rely on CTL function. However, tumors can evade killing through incompletely understood mechanisms. Understanding tumor evasion mechanisms will enable new immunotherapy strategies. Tumor susceptibility to CTL killing depends on genetically encoded tumor-intrinsic factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C24-C27 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These are well-established concepts in tumor immunology that frame the study rationale. The statements accurately reflect current knowledge and gaps in the field.

results.result: Recent CRISPR/siRNA screens identified factors in CTL resistance including antigen presentation, IFN-γ/TNF-α pathways, and autophagy. Specific regulators include PBAF complex, schlafen 11, apelin receptor-JAK1, Fitm2, Ptpn2 (IFN-γ pathway); Ado, TRAF2, Rb1cc1, PRMT1, RIPK1 (TNF-α pathway). Most prior studies used depletion screens with lower dynamic range than enrichment screens. Some mechanisms are shared across cell types while others are cell-line-specific. Pan-cancer analysis showed mutations in antigen presentation/interferon signaling mainly in melanoma, bladder, gastric, and lung cancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C47 comprehensively review prior literature with appropriate citations. The distinction between depletion and enrichment screens (C41-C42) provides important methodological context. The discussion of cell-type specificity (C47) and cancer-type patterns (C46) is well-supported by cited studies. This establishes the foundation for the current study's novelty.

results.result: This is the first study combining CRISPRa and CRISPR KO screens to study tumor-intrinsic determinants of CTL killing. The complementary approach enables study of genes not expressed endogenously at high levels. External peptide loading allows mapping of genes beyond antigen processing/presentation pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49, C168-C170 establish the study's novelty and advantages. The novelty claim (C48) appears accurate based on the literature review. The advantages of the complementary approach (C49, C169) are logical and demonstrated by the ability to identify genes like CD80 that aren't endogenously expressed. The peptide loading rationale (C170) explains the absence of antigen presentation hits and is a valid experimental design choice.

results.result: Expanded CMV-specific CTLs expressed CD25 (19.47±2.85%), PD-1 (29.49±0.55%), and LAG-3 (66.69±8.93%), displaying a more exhausted T cell phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 characterize the CTL phenotype with quantitative data. The expression of exhaustion markers (PD-1, LAG-3) is well-documented. The interpretation as "exhausted phenotype" (C61) is consistent with established knowledge about these markers. However, functional exhaustion (reduced cytokine production, proliferation) is not directly tested, only inferred from marker expression.
